Lower Bounds for Nonconvex-Concave Minimax Optimization

Qilong Wu The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen qilongwu@link.cuhk.edu.cn Zhihao Gu The Pennsylvania State University zbg5155@psu.edu Junchi Yang† The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen yangjunchi@cuhk.edu.cn
Abstract

We study lower bounds on the first-order oracle complexity of smooth nonconvex–concave minimax optimization. We consider objectives ff that are jointly LL-smooth in the primal and dual variables (𝒙,𝒚)(\bm{x},\bm{y}), concave in 𝒚\bm{y}, and whose primal value function Φ⁡(𝒙):=max𝒚∈𝒴⁡f⁡(𝒙,𝒚)\Phi(\bm{x}):=\max_{\bm{y}\in\mathcal{Y}}f(\bm{x},\bm{y}) satisfies the initial-gap condition Φ⁡(𝟎)−inf𝒙∈𝒳Φ⁡(𝒙)≤ΔΦ\Phi(\bm{0})-\inf_{\bm{x}\in\mathcal{X}}\Phi(\bm{x})\leq\Delta_{\Phi}, with a bounded dual domain satisfying diam⁡(𝒴)≤D𝒴\operatorname{diam}(\mathcal{Y})\leq D_{\mathcal{Y}}. We measure stationarity by the norm of the gradient of the Moreau envelope of Φ+ι𝒳\Phi+\iota_{\mathcal{X}} with parameter 1/(2​L)1/(2L). We prove that any deterministic zero-respecting first-order algorithm requires Ω⁡(L2​D𝒴​ΔΦ​ϵ−3)\Omega\!\left(L^{2}D_{\mathcal{Y}}\Delta_{\Phi}\,\epsilon^{-3}\right) oracle evaluations to find an ϵ\epsilon-stationary point. Under an unbiased stochastic first-order oracle with bounded variance, any stochastic zero-respecting algorithm requires Ω⁡(L3​D𝒴2​ΔΦ​ϵ−6)\Omega\!\left(L^{3}D_{\mathcal{Y}}^{2}\Delta_{\Phi}\,\epsilon^{-6}\right) oracle evaluations. The same lower bounds hold when ΔΦ\Delta_{\Phi} is replaced by the initial primal–dual gap 𝒢0\mathcal{G}_{0}. These deterministic and stochastic lower bounds match the corresponding upper bounds of [14] and [29], respectively, up to a logarithmic factor in the deterministic setting.

1 Introduction

Minimax optimization provides a common formulation for a broad range of problems in machine learning, statistics, and robust decision making. Such problems arise in applications including two-player zero-sum games [24], generative modeling [8], reinforcement learning [21, 27], robust and adversarial machine learning [15, 22], and robust optimization [2]. Optimization of pointwise maxima of nonconvex losses can also be written as a minimax problem through a dual representation [30]. A canonical formulation is

min𝒙∈𝒳⁡max𝒚∈𝒴⁡f⁡(𝒙,𝒚),\min_{\bm{x}\in\mathcal{X}}\max_{\bm{y}\in\mathcal{Y}}f(\bm{x},\bm{y}), (1)

where 𝒙\bm{x} denotes the model or decision variable and 𝒚\bm{y} represents an adversary, perturbation, or dual variable. A substantial part of the recent complexity theory has focused on the nonconvex–strongly-concave (NC–SC) setting, for which the first-order complexity is now relatively well understood: near-optimal algorithms and matching lower bounds, up to logarithmic factors, are known under standard smoothness assumptions [14, 11, 28].

The strong-concavity assumption, however, can be restrictive in applications. In many adversarial and robust formulations, the inner problem is naturally concave but has no intrinsic strongly concave curvature. This motivates the more general nonconvex–concave (NC–C) setting, where f⁡(𝒙,⋅)f(\bm{x},\cdot) is assumed only concave and the dual geometry is typically controlled through a bounded feasible set 𝒴\mathcal{Y}, for example with diam⁡(𝒴)≤D𝒴\operatorname{diam}(\mathcal{Y})\leq D_{\mathcal{Y}}. Define the primal value function

Φ⁡(𝒙):=max𝒚∈𝒴⁡f⁡(𝒙,𝒚),\Phi(\bm{x}):=\max_{\bm{y}\in\mathcal{Y}}f(\bm{x},\bm{y}),

and its extended value function φ:=Φ+ι𝒳\varphi:=\Phi+\iota_{\mathcal{X}}. Under LL-Lipschitz smoothness assumption on ff, φ\varphi is LL-weakly convex. A standard stationarity measure for NC–C minimax optimization is based on the Moreau envelope of φ\varphi, defined by

φλ​(𝒙):=min𝒛∈ℝdx⁡{φ⁡(𝒛)+12​λ​‖𝒛−𝒙‖2},0<λ<L−1.\varphi_{\lambda}(\bm{x}):=\min_{\bm{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}}\left\{\varphi(\bm{z})+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|\bm{z}-\bm{x}\|^{2}\right\},\qquad 0<\lambda<L^{-1}. (2)

The envelope φλ\varphi_{\lambda} is continuously differentiable for such λ\lambda, even when Φ\Phi itself is not. The literature has focused on finding an ϵ\epsilon-stationary point 𝒙\bm{x} satisfying

‖∇φλ​(𝒙)‖≤ϵ,\|\nabla\varphi_{\lambda}(\bm{x})\|\leq\epsilon, (3)

or the corresponding expected stationarity criterion in the stochastic setting [6, 23, 14, 25, 10, 29].

Despite substantial progress on algorithms for NC–C minimax optimization, considerably less is known about its fundamental oracle complexity. The best-known first-order methods achieve O~​(ϵ−3)\widetilde{O}(\epsilon^{-3}) gradient evaluations in the deterministic setting [14] and O⁡(ϵ−6)O(\epsilon^{-6}) stochastic gradient evaluations under a bounded-variance oracle [29]. In contrast, general lower bounds for NC–C minimax optimization remain much less developed. Since the NC–C class contains smooth nonconvex minimization and NC–SC minimax optimization as special cases, lower bounds for these problems immediately carry over to the NC–C setting. However, such inherited lower bounds do not match the best-known NC–C upper bounds. Existing lower-bound results tailored specifically to NC–C problems are instead largely algorithm-specific: they establish tight complexity guarantees for particular update rules, such as GDA, OGDA, extragradient, and perturbed or smoothed variants of GDA [16, 12], rather than for a broad class of zero-respecting first-order methods.

1.1 Our Contributions and Main Results

We establish oracle lower bounds for zero-respecting first-order algorithms. These bounds match the best-known upper bounds [14, 29], up to a logarithmic factor in the deterministic setting. Table 1 summarizes the resulting complexity landscape. Our main contributions are as follows:

  • •

    Oracle lower bounds for NC–C minimax optimization. We establish oracle lower bounds of Ω⁡(L2​D𝒴​ϵ−3)\Omega(L^{2}D_{\mathcal{Y}}\epsilon^{-3}) in the deterministic setting and Ω⁡(L3​D𝒴2​ϵ−6)\Omega(L^{3}D_{\mathcal{Y}}^{2}\epsilon^{-6}) in the stochastic setting. Both bounds hold under either of two standard initial-gap conditions: a bounded initial primal–dual gap or a bounded initial gap measured through the Moreau envelope of the primal value function. The deterministic lower bound matches the upper bound of [14] up to logarithmic factors, while the stochastic lower bound tightly matches the upper bound of [29]. These results characterize its intrinsic difficulty relative to smooth nonconvex minimization and NC–SC minimax optimization.

  • •

    A bounded zero-chain construction. The deterministic lower bound is based on a sequence of primal coordinates coupled through dual blocks: each successive primal coordinate can become nonzero only after first-order information has propagated through the intervening dual block. The construction is scaled so that the unconstrained dual maximizer lies in the interior of the prescribed bounded dual domain and the primal value function admits an exact representation. Moreover, the joint gradient is Lipschitz continuous with a constant independent of the chain dimensions, while the norm of the Moreau-envelope gradient remains bounded away from zero whenever the terminal primal coordinate is zero. Thus, the construction combines the standard nonconvex zero-chain obstruction with the additional oracle cost required for first-order information to propagate through the dual variables.

  • •

    A stochastic dual-gate mechanism. For the stochastic lower bound, we replace the quadratic difference terms (yk−yk+1)2(y_{k}-y_{k+1})^{2} along each dual block with clipped quadratic terms. This modification preserves both the primal value function and the dual maximizers, while uniformly bounding the gradient components corresponding to y2(i),…,yN(i)y_{2}^{(i)},\ldots,y_{N}^{(i)} in each dual block. We apply Bernoulli randomization only to these coordinates, leaving y1(i)y_{1}^{(i)} and all primal coordinates deterministic. After contracting the deterministic transitions, the progress analysis reduces to a probability-pp zero-chain over randomized dual coordinates. This yields the stochastic lower bound without imposing a uniform bound on the full dual gradient.

1.2 Related Work

Lower bounds for smooth nonconvex optimization.

Lower bounds for first-order optimization have a long history dating back to the information-based complexity framework of Nemirovski and Yudin [17]. In the noiseless convex setting, oracle complexity is well understood for a broad range of smooth [18] and nonsmooth [17] problems. A common approach is to construct high-dimensional instances for which each oracle call reveals only limited information about the solution. This idea appears in several forms, including resisting-oracle arguments, linear-span restrictions, and zero-respecting constructions. Zero-respecting constructions are particularly useful for nonconvex problems, where the hard instance can be organized as a chain whose coordinates must be revealed sequentially.

For smooth high-dimensional nonconvex optimization, Carmon et al. [3, 4] establish essentially tight first-order lower bounds for finding stationary points. For an LL-smooth function with initial function gap at most Δ\Delta, their results imply that Ω⁡(L​Δ​ϵ−2)\Omega\!\left(L\Delta\epsilon^{-2}\right) first-order oracle evaluations are necessary in the worst case to find an 𝒙\bm{x} satisfying ‖∇F​(𝒙)‖≤ϵ\|\nabla F(\bm{x})\|\leq\epsilon. This bound matches the complexity of gradient descent up to constants under the standard normalization. Their construction has a sequential zero-chain structure: before the algorithm reveals a given coordinate, the oracle provides no information about subsequent coordinates. This zero-respecting framework has become a standard tool for proving lower bounds in high-dimensional nonconvex optimization and is also the starting point of the hard instance developed in this paper. In stochastic nonconvex optimization, Arjevani et al. [1] combine deterministic nonconvex zero-chains with stochastic oracle constructions to obtain sharp lower bounds under bounded-variance and mean-squared-smoothness assumptions. Under a bounded-variance stochastic gradient oracle, the worst-case complexity can scale as Ω⁡(ϵ−4)\Omega(\epsilon^{-4}), whereas mean-squared smoothness leads to the characteristic ϵ−3\epsilon^{-3} dependence. These results show that the zero-chain framework applies to both deterministic and stochastic oracle models.

Lower bounds for minimax optimization.

For convex–concave saddle-point problems, lower complexity bounds were established using primal–dual hard instances in which information propagates alternately between the two variable blocks [19, 26]. For nonconvex–strongly-concave (NC–SC) minimax optimization, Zhang et al. [28] established lower bounds of Ω⁡(L​Δ​κ​ϵ−2)\Omega\!\left(L\Delta\sqrt{\kappa}\,\epsilon^{-2}\right) in the deterministic setting and Ω⁡(L​Δ​κ​ϵ−2+κ1/3​σ2​ϵ−4)\Omega\!\left(L\Delta\sqrt{\kappa}\,\epsilon^{-2}+\kappa^{1/3}\sigma^{2}\epsilon^{-4}\right) in the stochastic setting. Although NC–SC problems form a subclass of NC–C problems, the lower bounds in [11, 28] cannot be directly extended to the NC–C setting by simply letting the strong-concavity parameter μ\mu tend to zero. In particular, increasing the condition number alone does not ensure that the dual maximizers remain within a domain of prescribed diameter. Imposing such a restriction on the dual domain may alter the induced primal value function and thereby invalidate the gradient lower bound established for the original construction. Likewise, rescaling the instance to enforce the diameter constraint changes both the smoothness and stationarity scales, leading to a weaker complexity lower bound than the one established here.

Upper bounds for NC–C minimax optimization.

We next review existing upper bounds for NC–C minimax optimization under the stationarity measure adopted in this paper, namely, the norm of the gradient of a Moreau envelope of the primal value function. In the deterministic setting, existing first-order methods achieve an essentially O~​(ϵ−3)\widetilde{O}(\epsilon^{-3}) complexity under this stationarity criterion. This rate was first attained by Thekumparampil et al. [23] using an inexact proximal-point method. It was subsequently achieved by several other approaches, including accelerated inexact proximal-point methods [14, 10], Catalyst-type schemes [25], and primal–dual smoothing methods for max-structured nonconvex optimization [30]. In the stochastic setting, Zhang et al. [29] proposed SAPD+, which achieves an O⁡(ϵ−6)O(\epsilon^{-6}) stochastic oracle complexity under a bounded-variance stochastic gradient oracle. Accordingly, the relevant upper-bound benchmarks are O~​(ϵ−3)\widetilde{O}(\epsilon^{-3}) in the deterministic setting and O⁡(ϵ−6)O(\epsilon^{-6}) in the stochastic setting.

2 Problem Setup

In this section, we first formalize the problem class, the stationarity measure, and the oracle model. We then introduce the two components used in both the deterministic and stochastic hard instances: the tridiagonal path matrix Bα,NB_{\alpha,N}, which defines the dual chain, and the smooth functions ν\nu and rr, which are used to construct the primal relay.

2.1 Function Class and Stationarity Measure

For a f:𝒳×𝒴→ℝf:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}, define its primal value function by

Φf​(𝒙):=max𝒚∈𝒴⁡f⁡(𝒙,𝒚),𝒙∈𝒳,\Phi_{f}(\bm{x}):=\max_{\bm{y}\in\mathcal{Y}}f(\bm{x},\bm{y}),\qquad\bm{x}\in\mathcal{X},

and its extended-valued version by φf:=Φf+ι𝒳\varphi_{f}:=\Phi_{f}+\iota_{\mathcal{X}} on the ambient primal space.

We first introduce the function classes for smooth nonconvex–concave minimax problems. The two classes differ in how the initial optimality gap is measured. The first bounds the initial gap of the primal value function, whereas the second bounds the primal–dual gap at the reference point (0,0)(0,0). The former is used in [14], while the latter is used in [29].

Definition 2.1 (NC–C function classes).

Given L,D𝒴>0L,D_{\mathcal{Y}}>0, consider continuously differentiable functions f:𝒳×𝒴→ℝf:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}, over all finite dimensions dx,dy∈ℕd_{x},d_{y}\in\mathbb{N}, where 𝒳⊂ℝdx\mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}} and 𝒴⊂ℝdy\mathcal{Y}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}} are nonempty closed convex sets with 0∈𝒳0\in\mathcal{X} and 0∈𝒴0\in\mathcal{Y}, satisfying:

  1. 1.

    ff is jointly LL-smooth on 𝒳×𝒴\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}:

    ‖∇f​(𝒙,𝒚)−∇f​(𝒙′,𝒚′)‖≤L​‖(𝒙,𝒚)−(𝒙′,𝒚′)‖,∀(𝒙,𝒚),(𝒙′,𝒚′)∈𝒳×𝒴.\|\nabla f(\bm{x},\bm{y})-\nabla f(\bm{x}^{\prime},\bm{y}^{\prime})\|\leq L\|(\bm{x},\bm{y})-(\bm{x}^{\prime},\bm{y}^{\prime})\|,\qquad\forall(\bm{x},\bm{y}),(\bm{x}^{\prime},\bm{y}^{\prime})\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}.
  2. 2.

    For every 𝒙∈𝒳\bm{x}\in\mathcal{X}, f⁡(𝒙,⋅)f(\bm{x},\cdot) is concave.

  3. 3.

    The dual domain satisfies: diam⁡(𝒴):=sup𝒚,𝒚′∈𝒴‖𝒚−𝒚′‖≤D𝒴\operatorname{diam}(\mathcal{Y}):=\sup_{\bm{y},\bm{y}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}}\|\bm{y}-\bm{y}^{\prime}\|\leq D_{\mathcal{Y}}.

  4. 4.

    The initial scale is parameterized in either of the following two ways:

    1. (i)

      For ΔΦ>0\Delta_{\Phi}>0, ℱNCC​(L,ΔΦ,D𝒴)\mathcal{F}_{\rm NCC}(L,\Delta_{\Phi},D_{\mathcal{Y}}) denotes the class of functions satisfying

      Φf​(𝟎)−inf𝒙∈𝒳Φf​(𝒙)≤ΔΦ;\Phi_{f}(\bm{0})-\inf_{\bm{x}\in\mathcal{X}}\Phi_{f}(\bm{x})\leq\Delta_{\Phi};
    2. (ii)

      For 𝒢0>0\mathcal{G}_{0}>0, ℱNCCpd​(L,𝒢0,D𝒴)\mathcal{F}_{\rm NCC}^{\rm pd}(L,\mathcal{G}_{0},D_{\mathcal{Y}}) denotes the class of functions satisfying

      max𝒚∈𝒴⁡f⁡(0,𝒚)−inf𝒙∈𝒳f⁡(𝒙,0)≤𝒢0.\max_{\bm{y}\in\mathcal{Y}}f(0,\bm{y})-\inf_{\bm{x}\in\mathcal{X}}f(\bm{x},0)\leq\mathcal{G}_{0}.

No convexity is imposed on f⁡(⋅,𝒚)f(\cdot,\bm{y}). Since 𝒴\mathcal{Y} is closed and has finite diameter in a finite-dimensional space, it is compact. The continuity of ff therefore ensures that the maximum defining Φf\Phi_{f} is attained for every 𝒙∈𝒳\bm{x}\in\mathcal{X}. These two quantities satisfy

Φf​(𝟎)−inf𝒙∈𝒳Φf​(𝒙)≤max𝒚∈𝒴⁡f⁡(0,𝒚)−inf𝒙∈𝒳f⁡(𝒙,0),\Phi_{f}(\bm{0})-\inf_{\bm{x}\in\mathcal{X}}\Phi_{f}(\bm{x})\leq\max_{\bm{y}\in\mathcal{Y}}f(0,\bm{y})-\inf_{\bm{x}\in\mathcal{X}}f(\bm{x},0),

because Φf​(𝒙)≥f⁡(𝒙,0)\Phi_{f}(\bm{x})\geq f(\bm{x},0) for every 𝒙∈𝒳\bm{x}\in\mathcal{X}. Thus, a bound on the initial primal–dual gap also bounds the initial primal value gap. We will present the lower bounds for both classes.

For λ>0\lambda>0 and 𝒙∈ℝdx\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}, define the constrained proximal set by

𝒫λ​(𝒙):=arg⁡min𝒑∈𝒳​{Φf​(𝒑)+12​λ​‖𝒑−𝒙‖2},Gλ​(𝒙,𝒑):=λ−1​(𝒙−𝒑),𝒑∈𝒫λ​(𝒙).\mathcal{P}_{\lambda}(\bm{x}):=\arg\min_{\bm{p}\in\mathcal{X}}\left\{\Phi_{f}(\bm{p})+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\left\lVert\bm{p}-\bm{x}\right\rVert^{2}\right\},\quad G_{\lambda}(\bm{x};\bm{p}):=\lambda^{-1}(\bm{x}-\bm{p}),\quad\bm{p}\in\mathcal{P}_{\lambda}(\bm{x}). (4)

The initial-gap condition implies that Φf\Phi_{f} is bounded below on 𝒳\mathcal{X}. Equivalently, the set 𝒫λ​(𝒙)\mathcal{P}_{\lambda}(\bm{x}) is the proximal set of the extended-value function φf\varphi_{f} at 𝒙\bm{x} with parameter λ\lambda on ℝdx\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}. Although ff is smooth, the primal value function Φf\Phi_{f} need not be differentiable because the dual maximizer may be nonunique. Nevertheless, joint LL-smoothness of ff implies that f⁡(⋅,𝒚)f(\cdot,\bm{y}) is LL-weakly convex for every 𝒚∈𝒴\bm{y}\in\mathcal{Y}. Consequently, φf\varphi_{f} is a proper, lower semicontinuous, and LL-weakly convex function. We next recall the standard Moreau-envelope regularity result for this class of functions.

Lemma 2.2 (Lemma 2.2 in [6]).

Let φ:ℝdx→ℝ∪{+∞}\varphi:\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\} be proper, lower semicontinuous, and LL-weakly convex. For every 0<λ<L−10<\lambda<L^{-1} and every 𝐱∈ℝdx\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}, the proximal problem has a unique minimizer, denoted by 𝐩λφ​(𝐱)\bm{p}_{\lambda}^{\varphi}(\bm{x}):

arg⁡min𝒑∈ℝdx​{φ⁡(𝒑)+12​λ​‖𝒑−𝒙‖2}={𝒑λφ​(𝒙)}.\arg\min_{\bm{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}}\left\{\varphi(\bm{p})+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\left\lVert\bm{p}-\bm{x}\right\rVert^{2}\right\}=\{\bm{p}_{\lambda}^{\varphi}(\bm{x})\}.

Moreover, the Moreau envelope

φλ​(𝒙):=min𝒑∈ℝdx⁡{φ⁡(𝒑)+12​λ​‖𝒑−𝒙‖2}\varphi_{\lambda}(\bm{x}):=\min_{\bm{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}}\left\{\varphi(\bm{p})+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\left\lVert\bm{p}-\bm{x}\right\rVert^{2}\right\}

is continuously differentiable, and

∇φλ​(𝒙)=λ−1​(𝒙−𝒑λφ​(𝒙)).\nabla\varphi_{\lambda}(\bm{x})=\lambda^{-1}\bigl(\bm{x}-\bm{p}_{\lambda}^{\varphi}(\bm{x})\bigr). (5)

Applying Lemma 2.2 to φf=Φf+ι𝒳\varphi_{f}=\Phi_{f}+\iota_{\mathcal{X}}, we write 𝒑λ​(𝒙):=𝒑λφf​(𝒙)\bm{p}_{\lambda}(\bm{x}):=\bm{p}_{\lambda}^{\varphi_{f}}(\bm{x}). For 0<λ<L−10<\lambda<L^{-1}, this gives

𝒫λ​(𝒙)={𝒑λ​(𝒙)},∇(φf)λ​(𝒙)=Gλ​(𝒙,𝒑λ​(𝒙)).\mathcal{P}_{\lambda}(\bm{x})=\{\bm{p}_{\lambda}(\bm{x})\},\qquad\nabla(\varphi_{f})_{\lambda}(\bm{x})=G_{\lambda}\bigl(\bm{x};\bm{p}_{\lambda}(\bm{x})\bigr).

For both function classes, we measure stationarity using the gradient of the Moreau envelope of the value function, as defined below. This is a standard stationarity measure for weakly convex optimization [6, 7] and nonconvex–concave minimax optimization [29]. By Lemma 2.2, the corresponding stationarity conditions can equivalently be expressed in terms of G1/(2​L)​(𝒙,𝒑1/(2​L)​(𝒙)).G_{1/(2L)}\bigl(\bm{x};\bm{p}_{1/(2L)}(\bm{x})\bigr).

Definition 2.3.

Let f∈ℱNCC​(L,ΔΦ,D𝒴)∪ℱNCCpd​(L,𝒢0,D𝒴)f\in\mathcal{F}_{\rm NCC}(L,\Delta_{\Phi},D_{\mathcal{Y}})\cup\mathcal{F}_{\rm NCC}^{\rm pd}(L,\mathcal{G}_{0},D_{\mathcal{Y}}). A point 𝒙∈𝒳\bm{x}\in\mathcal{X} is ϵ\epsilon-stationary for the primal value function if

‖∇(φf)1/(2​L)​(𝒙)‖≤ϵ.\left\lVert\nabla(\varphi_{f})_{1/(2L)}(\bm{x})\right\rVert\leq\epsilon.

A random output 𝒙\bm{x} is expected ϵ\epsilon-stationary if

𝔼⁡‖∇(φf)1/(2​L)​(𝒙)‖≤ϵ.\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\nabla(\varphi_{f})_{1/(2L)}(\bm{x})\right\rVert\leq\epsilon.

2.2 Oracle and Algorithm Classes

We consider deterministic and stochastic first-order algorithms for nonconvex–concave minimax optimization. We begin by specifying the corresponding first-order oracle models.

Definition 2.4 (Deterministic first-order oracle).

The deterministic first-order oracle of a differentiable function f:𝒳×𝒴→ℝf:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is the mapping

𝒪ffo​(𝒙,𝒚)=(f⁡(𝒙,𝒚),∇𝒙f​(𝒙,𝒚),∇𝒚f​(𝒙,𝒚)),(𝒙,𝒚)∈𝒳×𝒴.\mathcal{O}_{f}^{\rm fo}(\bm{x},\bm{y})=(f(\bm{x},\bm{y}),\nabla_{\bm{x}}f(\bm{x},\bm{y}),\nabla_{\bm{y}}f(\bm{x},\bm{y})),\qquad(\bm{x},\bm{y})\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}.
Definition 2.5 (Stochastic first-order oracle).

The stochastic first-order oracle of a differentiable function f:𝒳×𝒴→ℝf:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} returns

𝒪fsfo​(𝒙,𝒚)=(f⁡(𝒙,𝒚),∇^𝒙​f​(𝒙,𝒚,ξ),∇^𝒚​f​(𝒙,𝒚,ξ)),(𝒙,𝒚)∈𝒳×𝒴,\mathcal{O}_{f}^{\rm sfo}(\bm{x},\bm{y})=(f(\bm{x},\bm{y}),\widehat{\nabla}_{\bm{x}}f(\bm{x},\bm{y};\xi),\widehat{\nabla}_{\bm{y}}f(\bm{x},\bm{y};\xi)),\qquad(\bm{x},\bm{y})\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y},

where ξ\xi is a random variable satisfying

𝔼ξ​[∇^​f​(𝒙,𝒚,ξ)]=∇f​(𝒙,𝒚),𝔼ξ​[‖∇^​f​(𝒙,𝒚,ξ)−∇f​(𝒙,𝒚)‖2]≤σ2.\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[\widehat{\nabla}f(\bm{x},\bm{y};\xi)]=\nabla f(\bm{x},\bm{y}),\qquad\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\left[\|\widehat{\nabla}f(\bm{x},\bm{y};\xi)-\nabla f(\bm{x},\bm{y})\|^{2}\right]\leq\sigma^{2}.

We restrict attention to zero-respecting first-order algorithms. Informally, such an algorithm can update only coordinates that have been revealed by previous first-order oracle responses. This class includes many standard first-order methods, including gradient descent–ascent, extragradient, and their standard momentum and stochastic variants [3, 11].

Definition 2.6 (Zero-respecting first-order algorithm).

A first-order algorithm is zero-respecting if, for every admissible function ff and every oracle transcript, the (t+1)(t+1)-th iterate (𝒙t+1,𝒚t+1)(\bm{x}^{t+1},\bm{y}^{t+1}) satisfies

𝒙t+1∈{𝖯𝒳​(𝒖):supp⁡(𝒖)⊆⋃0≤i≤t(supp⁡(𝒙i)∪supp⁡(∇𝒙f​(𝒙i,𝒚i)))},\bm{x}^{t+1}\in\left\{\mathsf{P}_{\mathcal{X}}(\bm{u}):\operatorname{supp}(\bm{u})\subseteq\bigcup_{0\leq i\leq t}\left(\operatorname{supp}(\bm{x}^{i})\cup\operatorname{supp}(\nabla_{\bm{x}}f(\bm{x}^{i},\bm{y}^{i}))\right)\right\},

and

𝒚t+1∈{𝖯𝒴​(𝒗):supp⁡(𝒗)⊆⋃0≤i≤t(supp⁡(𝒚i)∪supp⁡(∇𝒚f​(𝒙i,𝒚i)))}.\bm{y}^{t+1}\in\left\{\mathsf{P}_{\mathcal{Y}}(\bm{v}):\operatorname{supp}(\bm{v})\subseteq\bigcup_{0\leq i\leq t}\left(\operatorname{supp}(\bm{y}^{i})\cup\operatorname{supp}(\nabla_{\bm{y}}f(\bm{x}^{i},\bm{y}^{i}))\right)\right\}.

In the stochastic setting, the same condition is imposed pathwise with ∇𝒙f​(𝒙i,𝒚i)\nabla_{\bm{x}}f(\bm{x}^{i},\bm{y}^{i}) and ∇𝒚f​(𝒙i,𝒚i)\nabla_{\bm{y}}f(\bm{x}^{i},\bm{y}^{i}) replaced by the realized stochastic gradients ∇^𝒙​f​(𝒙i,𝒚i,ξi)\widehat{\nabla}_{\bm{x}}f(\bm{x}^{i},\bm{y}^{i};\xi_{i}) and ∇^𝒚​f​(𝒙i,𝒚i,ξi)\widehat{\nabla}_{\bm{y}}f(\bm{x}^{i},\bm{y}^{i};\xi_{i}), respectively.

Throughout, all algorithms are initialized at (𝒙0,𝒚0)=(0,0)(\bm{x}^{0},\bm{y}^{0})=(0,0), and the final primal output is also required to satisfy the same zero-respecting condition as the primal iterates. Since Euclidean projection onto each feasible set constructed in Section 3 preserves coordinate support, Definition 2.6 implies that every query is supported only on coordinates revealed by previous gradient evaluations. In the stochastic setting, the zero-respecting condition is imposed pathwise with respect to the realized stochastic gradients.

2.3 Zero-chain Framework

Zero-chain constructions are a standard tool for establishing first-order oracle lower bounds [3, 4, 1, 11, 9, 5]. To describe the sequential revelation of coordinates, for 𝒗∈ℝd\bm{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and θ≥0\theta\geq 0, define

progθ⁡(𝒗):=max⁡({j∈{1,…,d}:|vj|>θ}∪{0}).\operatorname{prog}_{\theta}(\bm{v}):=\max\Bigl(\{j\in\{1,\ldots,d\}:|v_{j}|>\theta\}\cup\{0\}\Bigr).

Thus, progθ⁡(𝒗)\operatorname{prog}_{\theta}(\bm{v}) is the largest index of a coordinate whose magnitude exceeds θ\theta, or zero if no such coordinate exists. In particular, prog0⁡(𝒗)\operatorname{prog}_{0}(\bm{v}) is the largest index in the support of 𝒗\bm{v}, with prog0⁡(0)=0\operatorname{prog}_{0}(0)=0.

Definition 2.7 (Zero-chain).

A differentiable function f:𝒳⊆ℝd→ℝf:\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} is a first-order zero-chain if, for every 𝒙∈𝒳\bm{x}\in\mathcal{X},

prog0⁡(∇f​(𝒙))≤min⁡{prog0⁡(𝒙)+1,d}.\operatorname{prog}_{0}(\nabla f(\bm{x}))\leq\min\{\operatorname{prog}_{0}(\bm{x})+1,d\}.

This condition ensures that a gradient evaluation reveals no coordinate with index greater than prog0⁡(𝒙)+1\operatorname{prog}_{0}(\bm{x})+1. The following stochastic analogue additionally bounds the probability of revealing that next coordinate.

Definition 2.8 (Probability-pp zero-chain).

Let p∈(0,1]p\in(0,1], and let f:𝒳⊆ℝd→ℝf:\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} be a differentiable function equipped with a stochastic first-order oracle 𝒪fsfo​(𝒙)=(f⁡(𝒙),∇^​f​(𝒙,ξ))\mathcal{O}_{f}^{\rm sfo}(\bm{x})=\bigl(f(\bm{x}),\widehat{\nabla}f(\bm{x};\xi)\bigr). We call ff a probability-pp zero-chain with respect to this oracle if, for every 𝒙∈𝒳\bm{x}\in\mathcal{X} with r:=prog0⁡(𝒙)<dr:=\operatorname{prog}_{0}(\bm{x})<d,

ℙξ​(prog0⁡(∇^​f​(𝒙,ξ))=r+1)≤p,ℙξ​(prog0⁡(∇^​f​(𝒙,ξ))>r+1)=0.\mathbb{P}_{\xi}\!\left(\operatorname{prog}_{0}(\widehat{\nabla}f(\bm{x};\xi))=r+1\right)\leq p,\qquad\mathbb{P}_{\xi}\!\left(\operatorname{prog}_{0}(\widehat{\nabla}f(\bm{x};\xi))>r+1\right)=0.

Here, the probability is taken over the randomness of the oracle.

Thus, the stochastic gradient has no nonzero coordinate with index greater than r+1r+1 almost surely, and its (r+1)(r+1)st coordinate is nonzero with probability at most pp.

When Euclidean projection onto each feasible set preserves coordinate support, a zero-respecting algorithm initialized at the origin can reveal at most one new coordinate per oracle call on a deterministic zero-chain. After tt oracle calls, its next query and any admissible output are therefore supported on the first tt coordinates. After tt oracle calls, its next query and any admissible output are therefore supported on the first tt coordinates. To establish a deterministic lower bound, it thus suffices to construct a zero-chain in the target function class for which the stationarity measure exceeds ϵ\epsilon at every feasible point 𝒙\bm{x} satisfying prog0⁡(𝒙)<T\operatorname{prog}_{0}(\bm{x})<T. Any zero-respecting algorithm must then make at least TT oracle calls to obtain an ϵ\epsilon-stationary point. For a probability-pp zero-chain, each oracle call reveals a new coordinate with conditional probability at most pp, given the preceding oracle transcript and the current query. Consequently, revealing the first TT coordinates requires Ω⁡(T/p)\Omega(T/p) oracle calls in expectation.

2.4 Component Functions

We now introduce several functions that will serve as building blocks for the hard instance constructed later. We also establish some of their key properties, which provide intuition for how these functions are used in the construction.

Quadratic chain.

Following [18, 4], for α>0\alpha>0 and an integer N≥2N\geq 2, define the tridiagonal matrix

Bα,N:=[1+α2−1−12−1⋱⋱⋱−12−1−11]∈ℝN×N.B_{\alpha,N}:=\begin{bmatrix}1+\alpha^{2}&-1&&&\\ -1&2&-1&&\\ &\ddots&\ddots&\ddots&\\ &&-1&2&-1\\ &&&-1&1\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}. (6)

The associated quadratic function is

fα,N​(𝒙):=12​𝒙⊤​Bα,N​𝒙=α22​x12+12​∑k=1N−1(xk−xk+1)2.f_{\alpha,N}(\bm{x}):=\frac{1}{2}\bm{x}^{\top}B_{\alpha,N}\bm{x}=\frac{\alpha^{2}}{2}x_{1}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}(x_{k}-x_{k+1})^{2}. (7)

Each difference term couples two neighboring coordinates, while the term α2​x12/2\alpha^{2}x_{1}^{2}/2 ensures that Bα,NB_{\alpha,N} is positive definite. The tridiagonal structure implies that each gradient component depends only on the corresponding coordinate and its immediate neighbors. Our later construction includes the negative of this quadratic function in the dual variable, which is a concave term. Its structure restricts the propagation of first-order information along the dual path and allows the dual maximizer to be computed explicitly.

Scalar component functions.

For nonconvex optimization, Carmon et al. [4] construct zero-chains using the smooth functions

Ψ¯(t):={0,t≤12,exp⁡(1−1(2​t−1)2),t>12,Φ¯(t):=e∫−∞te−s2/2ds.\bar{\Psi}(t):=\begin{cases}0,&t\leq\frac{1}{2},\\ \exp\left(1-\frac{1}{(2t-1)^{2}}\right),&t>\frac{1}{2},\end{cases}\qquad\bar{\Phi}(t):=\sqrt{e}\int_{-\infty}^{t}e^{-s^{2}/2}\,ds. (8)

The function Ψ¯\bar{\Psi} vanishes below a fixed threshold, which restricts when one coordinate can affect the gradient of the next. In our minimax instance construction, we want the dual maximizers to remain within a prescribed bounded domain while retaining a stationarity lower bound for the value function that is independent of the chain length. A direct rescaling of an unconstrained zero-chain from [4] does not guarantee both properties. We therefore introduce two continuously differentiable functions:

ν⁡(t):={0,t≤0,3​t2−2​t3,0<t<1,1,t≥1,r⁡(t):={t,t≤0,t⁡(1−t),0<t<1,1−t,t≥1.\nu(t):=\begin{cases}0,&t\leq 0,\\ 3t^{2}-2t^{3},&0<t<1,\\ 1,&t\geq 1,\end{cases}\qquad r(t):=\begin{cases}t,&t\leq 0,\\ t(1-t),&0<t<1,\\ 1-t,&t\geq 1.\end{cases} (9)

The function ν\nu is the cubic transition function used in previous zero-chain constructions [20]. It takes values in [0,1][0,1], equals zero on (−∞,0](-\infty,0], and equals one on [1,∞)[1,\infty). We use it to couple successive primal coordinates without introducing a direct gradient contribution at a coordinate equal to zero, since ν′​(0)=0\nu^{\prime}(0)=0.

The function rr has zeros at 00 and 11, and satisfies r′​(0)=1r^{\prime}(0)=1. In the hard instance, this nonzero derivative allows an auxiliary variable to produce a nonzero gradient at the next primal coordinate even when that coordinate is zero. The following lemma summarizes the key properties of these two functions. Its proof is deferred to Appendix A.1.

Lemma 2.9.

The functions ν\nu and rr are C1,1C^{1,1} and satisfy

|ν′|≤32,|ν′′|≤6,|r′|≤1,|r′′|≤2,|\nu^{\prime}|\leq\frac{3}{2},\qquad|\nu^{\prime\prime}|\leq 6,\qquad|r^{\prime}|\leq 1,\qquad|r^{\prime\prime}|\leq 2, (10)

where the second-derivative bounds hold almost everywhere. Moreover,

ν⁡(0)=ν′​(0)=r⁡(0)=0,r′​(0)=1,ν′​(t)=6​r​(t),0<t<1.\nu(0)=\nu^{\prime}(0)=r(0)=0,\qquad r^{\prime}(0)=1,\qquad\nu^{\prime}(t)=6r(t),\quad 0<t<1. (11)

For every κ∈(0,1/8)\kappa\in(0,1/8), if t≤2​κt\leq 2\kappa, then

ν⁡(t)≤2​|r⁡(t)|,r′​(t)≥1−4​κ,\nu(t)\leq 2|r(t)|,\qquad r^{\prime}(t)\geq 1-4\kappa,

and if t≥1−2​κt\geq 1-2\kappa, then

1−ν⁡(t)≤2​|r⁡(t)|.1-\nu(t)\leq 2|r(t)|.

The derivative bounds are used to establish smoothness of the hard instance. The remaining inequalities relate the values and derivatives of the component functions near the two thresholds 00 and 11; they are used to prove the stationarity lower bound before the terminal primal coordinate is revealed.

Normalized coupling between primal coordinates.

Fix an integer T≥2T\geq 2. For 𝒖∈ℝT\bm{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{T}, define 𝒒⁡(𝒖)=(q1​(𝒖),…,qT−1​(𝒖))\bm{q}(\bm{u})=(q_{1}(\bm{u}),\ldots,q_{T-1}(\bm{u})) by

qi(𝒖):=ν(ui)(1−ν(ui+1)),i=1,…,T−1.q_{i}(\bm{u}):=\nu(u_{i})\bigl(1-\nu(u_{i+1})\bigr),\qquad i=1,\ldots,T-1. (12)

Each component depends only on two successive coordinates. In particular, qi​(𝒖)=0q_{i}(\bm{u})=0 if ui≤0u_{i}\leq 0 or ui+1≥1u_{i+1}\geq 1, whereas qi​(𝒖)=1q_{i}(\bm{u})=1 if ui≥1u_{i}\geq 1 and ui+1≤0u_{i+1}\leq 0. Thus, 𝒒\bm{q} identifies transitions from a coordinate above the upper threshold to a subsequent coordinate below the lower threshold. Such a transition is central to the stationarity argument when the first primal coordinate is near or above 11 but the terminal coordinate is still zero.

Although each component of 𝒒\bm{q} is bounded by one, its Euclidean norm can grow with TT. We therefore define

𝝆⁡(𝒖):=𝒒⁡(𝒖)1+‖𝒒⁡(𝒖)‖2,\bm{\rho}(\bm{u}):=\frac{\bm{q}(\bm{u})}{\sqrt{1+\left\lVert\bm{q}(\bm{u})\right\rVert^{2}}},

so that

‖𝝆⁡(𝒖)‖≤1,𝒖∈ℝT.\left\lVert\bm{\rho}(\bm{u})\right\rVert\leq 1,\qquad\bm{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{T}. (13)

This uniform bound allows 𝝆\bm{\rho} to be coupled to auxiliary primal variables whose feasible radius is independent of TT. The normalization preserves the zero coordinates of 𝒒\bm{q}. Moreover, if uj=0u_{j}=0, then ν′​(uj)=0\nu^{\prime}(u_{j})=0, so the jjth column of D​𝒒​(𝒖)D\bm{q}(\bm{u}), and hence of D​𝝆​(𝒖)D\bm{\rho}(\bm{u}), vanishes. This property is used to verify that the normalized coupling preserves the required zero-chain structure.

The next lemma gives uniform bounds on the Jacobians of 𝒒\bm{q} and 𝝆\bm{\rho}, where DD denotes the Jacobian. All constants are independent of TT, which is essential for obtaining a smoothness bound independent of the dimensions of the hard instance. The proof is given in Appendix A.2.

Lemma 2.10.

For all 𝐮,𝐯∈ℝT\bm{u},\bm{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{T},

‖D​𝒒​(𝒖)‖op≤3,‖D​𝒒​(𝒖)−D​𝒒​(𝒗)‖op≤17​‖𝒖−𝒗‖,\left\lVert D\bm{q}(\bm{u})\right\rVert_{\rm op}\leq 3,\qquad\left\lVert D\bm{q}(\bm{u})-D\bm{q}(\bm{v})\right\rVert_{\rm op}\leq 17\left\lVert\bm{u}-\bm{v}\right\rVert,

and

‖D​𝝆​(𝒖)‖op≤3,‖D​𝝆​(𝒖)−D​𝝆​(𝒗)‖op≤71​‖𝒖−𝒗‖.\left\lVert D\bm{\rho}(\bm{u})\right\rVert_{\rm op}\leq 3,\qquad\left\lVert D\bm{\rho}(\bm{u})-D\bm{\rho}(\bm{v})\right\rVert_{\rm op}\leq 71\left\lVert\bm{u}-\bm{v}\right\rVert.

3 The Hard Instance

In this section, we first construct the deterministic hard instance and then establish the properties needed to prove both the deterministic and stochastic lower bounds.

3.1 Construction of the Hard Instance

The hard instance is constructed as the sum of primal and dual components. The primal component depends only on the primal variables and forms a chain along the primal coordinates. The dual component depends on both the primal and dual variables; it forms a chain along the dual coordinates while coupling the dual part to the primal chain [11, 9, 5].

Primal components.

Fix T,N≥2T,N\geq 2. The primal variables are 𝒖~∈ℝT,𝒂~,𝒃~∈ℝT−1\tilde{\bm{u}}\in\mathbb{R}^{T},\,\,\tilde{\bm{a}},\tilde{\bm{b}}\in\mathbb{R}^{T-1}, with feasible domain

C0:=ℝT×{(𝒂~,𝒃~)∈ℝT−1×ℝT−1:‖𝒂~‖2+‖𝒃~‖2≤R2},C_{0}:=\mathbb{R}^{T}\times\left\{(\tilde{\bm{a}},\tilde{\bm{b}})\in\mathbb{R}^{T-1}\times\mathbb{R}^{T-1}:\|\tilde{\bm{a}}\|^{2}+\|\tilde{\bm{b}}\|^{2}\leq R^{2}\right\}, (14)

where R>0R>0 is a universal constant. Using the relay function rr defined in (9), define 𝒓¯​(𝒖~):=(r⁡(u~2),…,r⁡(u~T))\bar{\bm{r}}(\tilde{\bm{u}}):=(r(\tilde{u}_{2}),\ldots,r(\tilde{u}_{T})). Then, the primal component function Ψ0:ℝT×ℝT−1×ℝT−1→ℝ\Psi_{0}:\mathbb{R}^{T}\times\mathbb{R}^{T-1}\times\mathbb{R}^{T-1}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is defined as

Ψ0​(𝒖~,𝒂~,𝒃~):=\displaystyle\Psi_{0}(\tilde{\bm{u}},\tilde{\bm{a}},\tilde{\bm{b}}):= H⁡(𝒖~)+12​‖𝒂~−𝝆⁡(𝒖~)‖2+12​‖𝒃~−𝒓¯​(𝒖~)‖2+12​(‖𝒂~‖2+‖𝒃~‖2),\displaystyle H(\tilde{\bm{u}})+\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert\tilde{\bm{a}}-\bm{\rho}(\tilde{\bm{u}})\right\rVert^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert\tilde{\bm{b}}-\bar{\bm{r}}(\tilde{\bm{u}})\right\rVert^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\bigl(\|\tilde{\bm{a}}\|^{2}+\|\tilde{\bm{b}}\|^{2}\bigr), (15)

where cη>0c_{\eta}>0 is a universal constant. The function H:ℝT→ℝH:\mathbb{R}^{T}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is defined as

H⁡(𝒖~):=−cη​u~1−cη​∑j=2Tν⁡(u~j)+cη2​∑j=1Tr​(u~j)2.H(\tilde{\bm{u}}):=-c_{\eta}\tilde{u}_{1}-c_{\eta}\sum_{j=2}^{T}\nu(\tilde{u}_{j})+\frac{c_{\eta}}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{T}r(\tilde{u}_{j})^{2}.

As illustrated in Figure 1, the two quadratic coupling terms connect successive primal coordinates through the auxiliary variables u~i\tilde{u}_{i}. The term 12​‖𝒂~−𝝆⁡(𝒖~)‖2\frac{1}{2}\|\tilde{\bm{a}}-\bm{\rho}(\tilde{\bm{u}})\|^{2} couples u~i\tilde{u}_{i} to a~i\tilde{a}_{i} through ρi​(𝒖~)\rho_{i}(\tilde{\bm{u}}), while 12​‖𝒃~−𝒓¯​(𝒖~)‖2\frac{1}{2}\|\tilde{\bm{b}}-\bar{\bm{r}}(\tilde{\bm{u}})\|^{2} couples b~i\tilde{b}_{i} to u~i+1\tilde{u}_{i+1}. In particular, when u~i+1=0\tilde{u}_{i+1}=0, the latter term contributes −b~i-\tilde{b}_{i} to the partial derivative with respect to u~i+1\tilde{u}_{i+1}, since r⁡(0)=0r(0)=0 and r′​(0)=1r^{\prime}(0)=1. The shifted coordinates in the definition of 𝒓¯​(𝒖~)\bar{\bm{r}}(\tilde{\bm{u}}) therefore ensure that each auxiliary variable b~i\tilde{b}_{i} is coupled to the next primal coordinate.

The function H⁡(𝒖~)H(\tilde{\bm{u}}) ensures that this sequential dependence leads to a stationarity lower bound. Its linear term −cη​u~1-c_{\eta}\tilde{u}_{1} produces a nonzero gradient in the first primal coordinate at the origin. The terms involving ν\nu and r2r^{2} are used to show that, at a point with sufficiently small constrained stationarity residual, each coordinate of 𝒖~\tilde{\bm{u}} must lie either near zero or above a threshold close to one. The first coordinate must lie above this threshold. If the terminal coordinate remains zero, there must therefore be a transition between the two regions. The coupling terms rule out a small stationarity residual at such a transition, yielding the required lower bound before the terminal primal coordinate is revealed.

Dual components.

The dual variable consists of T−1T-1 path blocks 𝒚(i)∈ℝN\bm{y}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}. Set α:=N−1/2\alpha:=N^{-1/2}. The matrix Bα,NB_{\alpha,N} in (6) satisfies the positive-definite identity in (7). For a,b∈ℝa,b\in\mathbb{R}, the function hN:(ℝ×ℝ)×ℝN→ℝh_{N}:(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R})\times\mathbb{R}^{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is defined as

hN​(a,b,𝒚):=ℓ0​[−12​𝒚⊤​Bα,N​𝒚+(α​a​𝒆1−α2​b​𝒆N)⊤​𝒚−α2​(N−1)8​b2],h_{N}(a,b;\bm{y}):=\ell_{0}\left[-\frac{1}{2}\bm{y}^{\top}B_{\alpha,N}\bm{y}+\left(\alpha a\bm{e}_{1}-\frac{\alpha}{2}b\bm{e}_{N}\right)^{\top}\bm{y}-\frac{\alpha^{2}(N-1)}{8}b^{2}\right], (16)

where ℓ0>0\ell_{0}>0 is a scaling parameter to be specified in the lower-bound theorems.

The tridiagonal matrix Bα,NB_{\alpha,N} couples neighboring dual coordinates, while the linear terms couple aa to y1y_{1} and bb to yNy_{N}. Thus, first-order information propagates from one endpoint to the other through the intervening dual coordinates. Together with the primal coupling terms in Ψ0\Psi_{0}, these dependencies give the zero-chain structure shown in Figure 1: a zero-respecting algorithm must reveal a block of NN dual coordinates before it can proceed to the next primal coordinate.

Rescaling and coupling the two components.

For a scaling parameter s>0s>0, define the primal and dual feasible sets by

X0:=ℝT×{(𝒂,𝒃)∈ℝT−1×ℝT−1:‖𝒂‖2+‖𝒃‖2≤(R​s)2},Y0:=D𝒴2​𝔹2(T−1)​N.X_{0}:=\mathbb{R}^{T}\times\left\{(\bm{a},\bm{b})\in\mathbb{R}^{T-1}\times\mathbb{R}^{T-1}:\left\lVert\bm{a}\right\rVert^{2}+\left\lVert\bm{b}\right\rVert^{2}\leq(Rs)^{2}\right\},\qquad Y_{0}:=\frac{D_{\mathcal{Y}}}{2}\mathbb{B}_{2}^{(T-1)N}. (17)

The variables 𝒖\bm{u} are unconstrained, whereas the auxiliary variables (𝒂,𝒃)(\bm{a},\bm{b}) lie in a Euclidean ball of radius R​sRs. This bound controls the norms of the unconstrained dual maximizers of the path blocks. With the parameter choices specified below, their concatenation lies in the interior of Y0Y_{0} for every feasible primal point. Consequently, restricting the dual maximization to Y0Y_{0} does not change its value.

For 𝒙=(𝒖,𝒂,𝒃)∈X0\bm{x}=(\bm{u},\bm{a},\bm{b})\in X_{0}, define the scaled variables

𝒖~:=𝒖/s,𝒂~:=𝒂/s,𝒃~:=𝒃/s.\tilde{\bm{u}}:=\bm{u}/s,\qquad\tilde{\bm{a}}:=\bm{a}/s,\qquad\tilde{\bm{b}}:=\bm{b}/s. (18)

Then (𝒖~,𝒂~,𝒃~)∈C0(\tilde{\bm{u}},\tilde{\bm{a}},\tilde{\bm{b}})\in C_{0}, so the scaled primal domain is independent of ss. The parameters ℓ0\ell_{0} and ss will be chosen to obtain the required smoothness and stationarity bounds while satisfying the dual feasibility condition.

We now define the hard instance f:(ℝT×ℝT−1×ℝT−1)×ℝ(T−1)​N→ℝf:\bigl(\mathbb{R}^{T}\times\mathbb{R}^{T-1}\times\mathbb{R}^{T-1}\bigr)\times\mathbb{R}^{(T-1)N}\to\mathbb{R} by

f⁡(𝒙,𝒚):=ℓ0​s2​Ψ0​(𝒖~,𝒂~,𝒃~)+∑i=1T−1hN​(ai,bi,𝒚(i)).f(\bm{x},\bm{y}):=\ell_{0}s^{2}\Psi_{0}(\tilde{\bm{u}},\tilde{\bm{a}},\tilde{\bm{b}})+\sum_{i=1}^{T-1}h_{N}(a_{i},b_{i};\bm{y}^{(i)}). (19)

Coordinate ordering.

We order the joint coordinates according to the dependencies shown in Figure 1. Starting from u1u_{1}, each stage passes through aia_{i}, the dual coordinates y1(i),…,yN(i)y_{1}^{(i)},\ldots,y_{N}^{(i)}, and bib_{i} before reaching ui+1u_{i+1}. The total number of coordinates is

K=1+(T−1)​(N+3).K=1+(T-1)(N+3). (21)

π1+(i−1)​(N+3)=ui,i=1,…,T,\pi_{1+(i-1)(N+3)}=u_{i},\qquad i=1,\ldots,T,

For a joint vector 𝒗\bm{v}, let [𝒗]πr[\bm{v}]_{\pi_{r}} denote its coordinate at position rr in the ordering 𝝅\bm{\pi} illustrated in Figure 1. For θ≥0\theta\geq 0, define

progθ𝝅⁡(𝒗):=max⁡({r∈{1,…,K}:|[𝒗]πr|>θ}∪{0}).\operatorname{prog}^{\bm{\pi}}_{\theta}(\bm{v}):=\max\Bigl(\{r\in\{1,\ldots,K\}:|[\bm{v}]_{\pi_{r}}|>\theta\}\cup\{0\}\Bigr). (22)

For a primal vector, we apply this definition after adjoining zero dual components, retaining the same joint coordinate ordering.

3.2 Structural Properties

We next establish the properties of the hard instance needed for the lower-bound analysis. These include an exact expression for the primal value function and its initial gap, a smoothness bound independent of the problem dimensions, and a stationarity lower bound when the terminal primal coordinate is zero.

We first analyze the dual maximization problem and the resulting primal value function. To state the value-function formula, define Ψ:ℝT×ℝT−1×ℝT−1→ℝ\Psi:\mathbb{R}^{T}\times\mathbb{R}^{T-1}\times\mathbb{R}^{T-1}\to\mathbb{R} by

Ψ⁡(𝒖~,𝒂~,𝒃~):=Ψ0​(𝒖~,𝒂~,𝒃~)+12​‖𝒂~−12​𝒃~‖2.\displaystyle\Psi(\tilde{\bm{u}},\tilde{\bm{a}},\tilde{\bm{b}}):=\Psi_{0}(\tilde{\bm{u}},\tilde{\bm{a}},\tilde{\bm{b}})+\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert\tilde{\bm{a}}-\frac{1}{2}\tilde{\bm{b}}\right\rVert^{2}. (23)

The following lemma shows that, under the stated feasibility condition, the unconstrained dual maximizer is unique and lies in the interior of Y0Y_{0} for every feasible primal point. Thus, restricting the dual maximization to Y0Y_{0} leaves its value unchanged. The lemma expresses Φ\Phi as a scaled version of Ψ\Psi and computes the exact initial value gap, which will be used to choose parameters satisfying the gap bound of the target function class. The proof is given in Appendix A.3.

    Φ⁡(𝒖,𝒂,𝒃)=ℓ0​s2​Ψ​(𝒖/s,𝒂/s,𝒃/s).\Phi(\bm{u},\bm{a},\bm{b})=\ell_{0}s^{2}\Psi(\bm{u}/s,\bm{a}/s,\bm{b}/s). (24)

    Φ⁡(0)−inf𝒙∈X0Φ⁡(𝒙)=cη​(T+12)​ℓ0​s2.\Phi(0)-\inf_{\bm{x}\in X_{0}}\Phi(\bm{x})=c_{\eta}\left(T+\frac{1}{2}\right)\ell_{0}s^{2}. (25)

The proof is given in Appendix A.4.

For every T,N≥2T,N\geq 2, every s>0s>0, and every ℓ0>0\ell_{0}>0, the hard instance (19) satisfies

‖∇f​(𝒛)−∇f​(𝒛′)‖≤Cℓ​ℓ0​‖𝒛−𝒛′‖for all ​𝒛,𝒛′∈X0×Y0,\left\lVert\nabla f(\bm{z})-\nabla f(\bm{z}^{\prime})\right\rVert\leq C_{\ell}\ell_{0}\left\lVert\bm{z}-\bm{z}^{\prime}\right\rVert\qquad\text{for all }\bm{z},\bm{z}^{\prime}\in X_{0}\times Y_{0}, (26)

Specifically, we show that the norm of the Moreau-envelope gradient remains bounded away from zero whenever the terminal primal coordinate is zero. 4 Lower Bound for Deterministic NC-C Minimax Optimization

We now derive the deterministic first-order oracle lower bound by specifying the parameters of the hard instance in (19). Using Lemmas 3.1–3.3, we choose ℓ0,s,T,N\ell_{0},s,T,N so that the instance satisfies the prescribed smoothness, initial-gap, and dual-diameter bounds, while the norm of the Moreau-envelope gradient exceeds ϵ\epsilon at every feasible primal point with uT=0u_{T}=0. The zero-chain property then implies that a zero-respecting algorithm must reveal the terminal primal coordinate before returning an ϵ\epsilon-stationary point. Counting the oracle calls required to reach this coordinate gives the following theorem. Its proof is given in Appendix B.1.

Theorem 4.1 (Deterministic zero-respecting lower bound).

There exist universal constants c0,c1>0c_{0},c_{1}>0 such that, for every L,ΔΦ,D𝒴>0L,\Delta_{\Phi},D_{\mathcal{Y}}>0 and every ϵ\epsilon satisfying

0<ϵ≤c1​min⁡{L​ΔΦ,L​D𝒴},0<\epsilon\leq c_{1}\min\{\sqrt{L\Delta_{\Phi}},\,LD_{\mathcal{Y}}\}, (31)

there is an instance f∈ℱNCC​(L,ΔΦ,D𝒴)f\in\mathcal{F}_{\rm NCC}(L,\Delta_{\Phi},D_{\mathcal{Y}}) on finite-dimensional closed convex sets X0,Y0X_{0},Y_{0}, with diam⁡(Y0)=D𝒴\operatorname{diam}(Y_{0})=D_{\mathcal{Y}}, for which the following lower bound holds. Let Φ⁡(𝐱):=max𝐲∈Y0⁡f⁡(𝐱,𝐲)\Phi(\bm{x}):=\max_{\bm{y}\in Y_{0}}f(\bm{x},\bm{y}) and φ:=Φ+ιX0\varphi:=\Phi+\iota_{X_{0}}. For any deterministic zero-respecting first-order algorithm, every zero-respecting primal output 𝐱∈X0\bm{x}\in X_{0} produced after qq joint oracle calls with

q<c0​L2​D𝒴​ΔΦ​ϵ−3q<c_{0}L^{2}D_{\mathcal{Y}}\Delta_{\Phi}\,\epsilon^{-3} (32)

satisfies

‖∇φ1/(2​L)​(𝒙)‖=‖G1/(2​L)​(𝒙,𝒑)‖>ϵ,\left\lVert\nabla\varphi_{1/(2L)}(\bm{x})\right\rVert=\left\lVert G_{1/(2L)}(\bm{x};\bm{p})\right\rVert>\epsilon, (33)

where 𝐩\bm{p} is the unique point in 𝒫1/(2​L)​(𝐱)\mathcal{P}_{1/(2L)}(\bm{x}). Consequently, the deterministic zero-respecting first-order oracle complexity of finding an ϵ\epsilon-stationary point is

Ω⁡(L2​D𝒴​ΔΦ​ϵ−3).\Omega\!\left(L^{2}D_{\mathcal{Y}}\Delta_{\Phi}\,\epsilon^{-3}\right).

Theorem 4.1 expresses the lower bound in terms of the initial primal value gap. For the hard instance constructed in its proof, this gap equals the initial primal–dual gap. Therefore, replacing ΔΦ\Delta_{\Phi} by 𝒢0\mathcal{G}_{0} in the same construction gives the corresponding lower bound for ℱNCCpd​(L,𝒢0,D𝒴)\mathcal{F}_{\rm NCC}^{\rm pd}(L,\mathcal{G}_{0},D_{\mathcal{Y}}). The proof of the following corollary is given in Appendix B.2.

Corollary 4.2.

There exists a universal constant c>0c>0 such that, for every L,𝒢0,D𝒴>0L,\mathcal{G}_{0},D_{\mathcal{Y}}>0 and every ϵ\epsilon satisfying

0<ϵ≤c​min⁡{L​𝒢0,L​D𝒴},0<\epsilon\leq c\min\{\sqrt{L\mathcal{G}_{0}},\,LD_{\mathcal{Y}}\},

there is an instance

f∈ℱNCCpd​(L,𝒢0,D𝒴)f\in\mathcal{F}_{\rm NCC}^{\rm pd}(L,\mathcal{G}_{0},D_{\mathcal{Y}})

on which every deterministic zero-respecting first-order algorithm requires

Ω⁡(L2​D𝒴​𝒢0​ϵ−3)\Omega\!\left(L^{2}D_{\mathcal{Y}}\mathcal{G}_{0}\,\epsilon^{-3}\right)

joint oracle evaluations to return an ϵ\epsilon-stationary point of the primal value function.

5 Lower Bound for Stochastic NC-C Minimax Optimization

We extend the deterministic construction to establish a lower bound under unbiased stochastic first-order oracles with bounded variance. The construction retains the same primal value function and the stationarity lower bound at points with uT=0u_{T}=0. We modify the dual blocks so that the gradient components corresponding to y2(i),…,yN(i)y_{2}^{(i)},\ldots,y_{N}^{(i)} are uniformly bounded, and apply Bernoulli randomization only to these coordinates. The coordinates y1(i)y_{1}^{(i)} and all primal coordinates are returned deterministically.

To reach the terminal primal coordinate, a zero-respecting algorithm must cross M=(T−1)​(N−1)M=(T-1)(N-1) randomized dual coordinates. Each such coordinate requires a successful Bernoulli trial, while the intervening deterministic transitions can be treated as free in the progress analysis. Combining this progress bound with the stationarity obstruction yields the stochastic oracle lower bound.

Throughout this section, we retain the notation and universal constants introduced in Section 3. In particular, we use the same primal functions Ψ0,Ψ\Psi_{0},\Psi, feasible sets C0,X0,Y0C_{0},X_{0},Y_{0}, coordinate ordering 𝝅\bm{\pi}, and chain length KK. We take α=N−1/2\alpha=N^{-1/2} and ℓ0=L/Cℓ\ell_{0}=L/C_{\ell}, using the same universal constant CℓC_{\ell} fixed in Appendix A.4. Only the dual blocks are modified.

5.1 Clipping the Dual Quadratic Terms

The stochastic oracle will randomize only the dual coordinates y2(i),…,yN(i)y_{2}^{(i)},\ldots,y_{N}^{(i)}. To control the variance of this oracle, we need a uniform bound on the corresponding gradient components. In the deterministic construction, the quadratic difference terms produce gradients whose magnitude depends on the neighboring dual coordinates, and the diameter bound on Y0Y_{0} alone does not provide the required dependence on NN. We therefore replace these terms with clipped quadratics.

For τ>0\tau>0, define

χτ​(t):={12​t2,|t|≤τ,τ​|t|−12​τ2,|t|>τ,χτ′​(t)={−τ,t<−τ,t,|t|≤τ,τ,t>τ.\chi_{\tau}(t):=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{2}t^{2},&|t|\leq\tau,\\[5.69054pt] \tau|t|-\frac{1}{2}\tau^{2},&|t|>\tau,\end{cases}\qquad\chi_{\tau}^{\prime}(t)=\begin{cases}-\tau,&t<-\tau,\\ t,&|t|\leq\tau,\\ \tau,&t>\tau.\end{cases} (34)

The function χτ\chi_{\tau} is convex and continuously differentiable, and its derivative satisfies

|χτ′(t)|≤τ,|χτ′(t)−χτ′(t′)|≤|t−t′|,t,t′∈ℝ.|\chi_{\tau}^{\prime}(t)|\leq\tau,\qquad|\chi_{\tau}^{\prime}(t)-\chi_{\tau}^{\prime}(t^{\prime})|\leq|t-t^{\prime}|,\qquad t,t^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}. (35)

The first bound controls the gradient contribution of each difference term, while the second provides the regularity needed for a smoothness bound independent of the problem dimensions. The function and its derivative are shown in Figure 2.

We choose the clipping threshold as

τN:=R​α​s.\tau_{N}:=R\alpha s. (36)

For the deterministic maximizer of a block with feasible endpoint parameters ai,bia_{i},b_{i}, every difference between neighboring dual coordinates equals α​bi/2\alpha b_{i}/2. Since |bi|≤R​s|b_{i}|\leq Rs, its magnitude is at most τN/2\tau_{N}/2. Thus, every such difference lies strictly inside the quadratic region of χτN\chi_{\tau_{N}}. The lemma below verifies that this choice preserves both the maximizer and the maximum value of each feasible block.

For scalar parameters a,b∈ℝa,b\in\mathbb{R}, we define the clipped dual block as

hNclip(a,b;𝒚):=ℓ0[−∑k=1N−1χτN(yk−yk+1)−α22y12+𝒄(a,b)⊤𝒚−α2​(N−1)8b2].h_{N}^{\rm clip}(a,b;\bm{y}):=\ell_{0}\left[-\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\chi_{\tau_{N}}(y_{k}-y_{k+1})-\frac{\alpha^{2}}{2}y_{1}^{2}+\bm{c}(a,b)^{\top}\bm{y}-\frac{\alpha^{2}(N-1)}{8}b^{2}\right]. (37)

where 𝒄⁡(a,b):=α​a​𝒆1−α2​b​𝒆N\bm{c}(a,b):=\alpha a\bm{e}_{1}-\frac{\alpha}{2}b\bm{e}_{N}. Replacing each deterministic dual block by this function gives

fsg​(𝒙,𝒚):=ℓ0​s2​Ψ0​(𝒖~,𝒂~,𝒃~)+∑i=1T−1hNclip​(ai,bi,𝒚(i)),𝒖~=𝒖s,𝒂~=𝒂s,𝒃~=𝒃s.f^{\rm sg}(\bm{x},\bm{y}):=\ell_{0}s^{2}\Psi_{0}(\tilde{\bm{u}},\tilde{\bm{a}},\tilde{\bm{b}})+\sum_{i=1}^{T-1}h_{N}^{\rm clip}(a_{i},b_{i};\bm{y}^{(i)}),\qquad\tilde{\bm{u}}=\frac{\bm{u}}{s},\quad\tilde{\bm{a}}=\frac{\bm{a}}{s},\quad\tilde{\bm{b}}=\frac{\bm{b}}{s}. (38)

We use the same feasible sets as in the deterministic construction:

X0=ℝT×{(𝒂,𝒃)∈ℝT−1×ℝT−1:‖𝒂‖2+‖𝒃‖2≤(R​s)2},Y0=D𝒴2​𝔹2(T−1)​N.X_{0}=\mathbb{R}^{T}\times\left\{(\bm{a},\bm{b})\in\mathbb{R}^{T-1}\times\mathbb{R}^{T-1}:\left\lVert\bm{a}\right\rVert^{2}+\left\lVert\bm{b}\right\rVert^{2}\leq(Rs)^{2}\right\},\qquad Y_{0}=\frac{D_{\mathcal{Y}}}{2}\mathbb{B}_{2}^{(T-1)N}.

Φsg​(𝒙):=max𝒚∈Y0⁡fsg​(𝒙,𝒚),𝒙∈X0,\Phi_{\rm sg}(\bm{x}):=\max_{\bm{y}\in Y_{0}}f^{\rm sg}(\bm{x},\bm{y}),\qquad\bm{x}\in X_{0}, (39)

The proof is given in Appendix C.1.

5.2 A Probability-pp Dual Zero-chain

We first recall two standard results for stochastic zero-chains.

Lemma 5.2 (Lemma 3 in [1]).

Let f:𝒳→ℝf:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} be a zero-chain on 𝒳⊂ℝT\mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{T}. For 𝐱∈𝒳\bm{x}\in\mathcal{X}, let i∗​(𝐱):=inf{i∈[T]:xi=0}i^{*}(\bm{x}):=\inf\{i\in[T]:x_{i}=0\} denote the next coordinate to be discovered. For p∈(0,1]p\in(0,1], define

6 Conclusion and Future Work

We established first-order oracle lower bounds for smooth nonconvex–concave minimax optimization within the class of zero-respecting algorithms. Under the primal-value-gap and primal–dual-gap parameterizations, the deterministic lower bounds are Ω⁡(L2​D𝒴​ΔΦ​ϵ−3)\Omega(L^{2}D_{\mathcal{Y}}\Delta_{\Phi}\,\epsilon^{-3}) and Ω⁡(L2​D𝒴​𝒢0​ϵ−3)\Omega(L^{2}D_{\mathcal{Y}}\mathcal{G}_{0}\,\epsilon^{-3}), respectively. In the stochastic setting, the corresponding lower bounds are Ω⁡(L3​D𝒴2​ΔΦ​σ2​ϵ−6)\Omega(L^{3}D_{\mathcal{Y}}^{2}\Delta_{\Phi}\sigma^{2}\,\epsilon^{-6}) and Ω⁡(L3​D𝒴2​𝒢0​σ2​ϵ−6)\Omega(L^{3}D_{\mathcal{Y}}^{2}\mathcal{G}_{0}\sigma^{2}\,\epsilon^{-6}). In their dependence on LL, D𝒴D_{\mathcal{Y}}, and ϵ\epsilon, these bounds match the deterministic upper bound of [14] up to a logarithmic factor and the stochastic upper bound of [29].

Several questions remain open:

Beyond zero-respecting algorithms.

Our lower bounds are proved for first-order zero-respecting methods. A natural next step is to determine whether the same rates hold for arbitrary, possibly randomized, first-order algorithms. In classical nonconvex optimization, zero-chain lower bounds can often be extended using random rotations or resisting-oracle arguments. Establishing an analogous reduction while preserving the primal–dual structure of the present construction is an important open problem.

Separate oracle complexities.

Our lower bounds concern the joint first-order oracle, where each query returns both ∇xf\nabla_{x}f and ∇yf\nabla_{y}f. It remains open whether the primal and dual gradient complexities differ when counted separately. The structure of our hard instance suggests possible primal and dual gradient complexities scaling as ϵ−2\epsilon^{-2} and ϵ−3\epsilon^{-3}, respectively, in the deterministic setting, and as ϵ−2\epsilon^{-2} and ϵ−6\epsilon^{-6} in the bounded-variance stochastic setting. The best-known existing algorithms, however, require the same order of primal and dual gradient evaluations. Resolving this question may require new lower-bound constructions tailored to separate primal and dual first-order oracles, new algorithms with improved primal or dual gradient complexity, or both. Such results would clarify whether existing joint-oracle methods are individually optimal in their use of primal and dual gradients.

ff-stationarity versus Φ\Phi-stationarity.

Recent algorithmic results have demonstrated that game stationarity and optimization stationarity may exhibit genuinely different complexity behavior [13, 12]. Our lower bounds concern stationarity of the value function Φ⁡(𝒙)=max𝒚∈𝒴⁡f⁡(𝒙,𝒚)\Phi(\bm{x})=\max_{\bm{y}\in\mathcal{Y}}f(\bm{x},\bm{y}). It remains open whether comparable lower bounds hold for stationarity notions defined directly in terms of the saddle function ff, such as ‖∇f‖\|\nabla f\|. Since an ff-stationary pair need not correspond to a nearly maximizing dual variable, the complexity of ff-stationarity may differ substantially from that of Φ\Phi-stationarity. Determining the tight complexity of the two notions, and whether a genuine separation exists between them, is an interesting open question.

NC–C Bilevel Optimization.

An important direction for future research is to extend the present lower-bound framework to NC–C bilevel optimization, for which general first-order complexity lower bounds remain open. A natural question is whether the primal–dual information propagation mechanism developed here can be transferred to this setting and used to establish lower bounds for NC–C bilevel problems.

AI Disclosure

The hard-instance construction was developed through iterative collaboration with OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra. The authors provided the model with an independently developed proof draft that already contained the central dual-chain construction, the ℓ2\ell_{2} constraint on the auxiliary primal variables, and the scaling argument underlying the ϵ−3\epsilon^{-3} deterministic lower bound. The model was then used to help identify and refine several composite functions in the primal component, which addressed a key obstacle in the original construction. For the stochastic lower bound, the authors independently introduced the stochastic dual zero-chain mechanism used in the final proof. Building on these ingredients, the model assisted in refining the construction and in developing several technical arguments, including parts of the clipping mechanism. The authors subsequently simplified and independently verified the resulting arguments and take full responsibility for the correctness and presentation of the paper. A Lean formalization, developed with Codex and available at https://github.com/Wu-Qilong/Lower-Bounds-for-Nonconvex-Concave-Minimax-Optimization, provides a formal verification.

C.4 Proof of Corollary 5.6

Proof.

Consider the stochastic hard instance used in Theorem 5.5. By Lemma 5.1, the clipped construction has the same primal value function as the deterministic construction:

Φsg​(𝒙)=Φf​(𝒙).\Phi_{\rm sg}(\bm{x})=\Phi_{f}(\bm{x}).

Moreover, since χτN​(0)=0\chi_{\tau_{N}}(0)=0, clipping does not change the objective at 𝒚=𝟎\bm{y}=\bm{0}:

fsg​(𝒙,𝟎)=f⁡(𝒙,𝟎).f^{\rm sg}(\bm{x},\bm{0})=f(\bm{x},\bm{0}).

Therefore the argument in the proof of Corollary 4.2 applies verbatim and gives

max𝒚∈Y0⁡fsg​(𝟎,𝒚)−inf𝒙∈X0fsg​(𝒙,𝟎)\displaystyle\max_{\bm{y}\in Y_{0}}f^{\rm sg}(\bm{0},\bm{y})-\inf_{\bm{x}\in X_{0}}f^{\rm sg}(\bm{x},\bm{0}) =Φsg​(𝟎)−inf𝒙∈X0Φsg​(𝒙).\displaystyle=\Phi_{\rm sg}(\bm{0})-\inf_{\bm{x}\in X_{0}}\Phi_{\rm sg}(\bm{x}).

Now apply Theorem 5.5 with ΔΦ=𝒢0\Delta_{\Phi}=\mathcal{G}_{0}. The common gap is at most 𝒢0\mathcal{G}_{0}, so the resulting instance belongs to ℱNCCpd​(L,𝒢0,D𝒴)\mathcal{F}_{\rm NCC}^{\rm pd}(L,\mathcal{G}_{0},D_{\mathcal{Y}}). The claimed oracle lower bound follows directly. ∎
